Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed offline pipeline. Given an input image, the frozen I-JEPA target encoder extracts a raw embedding, which is processed by the MLP projection head and the classification head to produce logits over the known generators. The logits are used to compute an energy score for open-set rejection: samples with low energy are accepted and attributed to one of the known generators, while high-energy samples are rejected as unknown. For rejected samples, the pipeline combines the projected I-JEPA representation with the corresponding FSD descriptor. The resulting fused representations are then clustered with HDBSCAN to discover and organize samples from unknown generators.

Fig. 16. UMAP visualizations of WILD open-set generator space using different embedding representations. Points are colored according to the ground-truth generator labels. (a) I-JEPA raw embeddings. (b) I-JEPA projected embeddings trained with CE. (c) I-JEPA projected embeddings trained with CE+SupCon. (d) FSD embeddings. (e) FSD + I-JEPA projected embeddings trained with CE. (f) FSD + I-JEPA projected embeddings trained with CE+SupCon. The comparison shows that raw I-JEPA embeddings are highly entangled, projected I-JEPA features improve generator-wise grouping, and FSD-based representations produce more compact and separated structures. The fused embeddings provide the clearest organization of the open-set space.

The comparison shows that most generators form compact groups, while the main errors are the split of Dall-E 1 into two separate groups and the overlap between Nvidia Sana PAG and Tencent Hunyuan.

This shows that energy-based rejection alone is not sufficient with post-processed images.
